v: West of Calgary, there's a reservoir that's meant to stay empty.
To understand why, go back to June twenty thirteen.
Heavy rain fell on melting snow in the Rocky Mountains, and both of Calgary's rivers rose.
The Bow River peaked at eight times its regular flow. The Elbow, at twelve times.
About eighty thousand people were evacuated, from twenty-six communities.
Downtown was inaccessible for days. At the Saddledome, at least the first ten rows were underwater.
One Calgarian lost their life. Across Alberta, the flood's impact was assessed at about five billion dollars.
So Calgary and the province started building.
At the Glenmore Dam, new steel gates, two and a half metres high, doubled the reservoir's storage.
Along the Bow, a permanent flood barrier was finished downtown. In September twenty twenty-six, another was completed for Sunnyside and Hillhurst.
And about fifteen kilometres west of the city, Alberta built the Springbank Off-stream Reservoir.
Most of the time, it's dry land. In a big flood, a channel diverts water from the Elbow River, stores it, and releases it back when it's safe.
It can store seventy point two million cubic metres. That's about twenty-eight thousand Olympic swimming pools.
The City says Elbow River communities are now protected from a flood the size of twenty thirteen, and that Calgary's flood risk is down by about seventy per cent.
The Bow is a different story. Its upstream reservoir option, a relocated Ghost Dam, is still in engineering and regulatory approvals.
Twenty thirteen changed how Calgary lives with its rivers.
